terms.def: A classic SQL injection: ' ends the input, OR 1=1 is always true, -- comments out the password check.
Check staff access and remove unnecessary permissions.
Sets clear expectations for how staff use IT systems securely.
Deciding who can access systems, files or data, and what they can do.
Key cards, biometric scanners or PINs unique to each person, so only pre-authorised people get in.
A record of who entered or accessed what, and when.
Sending sensitive information to the wrong person, or posting private information publicly.
Data shared by mistake. It damages the organisation's reputation and so its profitability.
GDPR principle: keep data correct and up to date, and fix mistakes quickly
Bombards users with pop-ups to make money, often tracking behaviour and installing unwanted programs.
Review security immediately and make improvements.
Devices with microphones or cameras that record continuously. If compromised, they enable eavesdropping.
A full physical security audit.
The route (path) or method an attacker uses to reach a system or a weakness.
A device that runs itself, e.g. self-driving cars, traffic light systems, central heating.
Editing databases or data stores, e.g. changing financial details or breaking how a system works.
A hidden way into a system that lets attackers bypass normal security.
A backup is a copy of data. Disaster recovery is the whole plan to get systems and the business running again.
When an AI system makes unfair or skewed decisions because of faulty or poisoned training data.
Using physical features such as fingerprints or facial recognition to unlock a secure area.
Exploited a Windows XP/2000 weakness, caused crashes and restarts, infected millions. Lesson: patch and use firewalls.
Short-range wireless for headphones and keyboards. Risks: unprotected pairing, malicious files.
Targets the master boot record (MBR) and loads into memory when the computer restarts. Signs: boot-up problems.
An infected computer secretly controlled by a hacker and used in attacks such as DDoS.
A large network of bot-infected computers secretly controlled by a hacker to attack on a massive scale.
A network of bots used together for a large-scale attack.
About 400,000 customers' details stolen; £20 million ICO fine; all four types of loss.
A user can access information or files they shouldn't.
Users can see or do things they shouldn't be allowed to.
Changes your homepage, new tab page or search engine and redirects you to malicious sites. Not technically a virus.
Used to steal usernames and passwords, including ones saved in the browser.
Burglar = threat; broken window lock = vulnerability; the window = attack vector.
The rule for access: only people who need it for their job should get into restricted areas.
Bring your own device: secures personal devices used on the network.
Income slows or stops while expenses carry on.
The four-step chain for strong exam answers about vulnerabilities.
Cameras that monitor entrances and restricted areas; footage is reviewed for suspicious activity.
Cameras at entrances, watched live by security staff who review suspicious activity.
Mobile networks. Risks: rogue base stations, SIM weaknesses.
Windows command to calculate a file's hash: certutil -hashfile [file path] SHA256.
Staff questioning unknown people, because they may be using impersonation or coercion to get in.
North Korean hackers used phishing and an unknown Chrome flaw to install spyware; Google issued an emergency patch.
Data sent without encryption, so it can be read if intercepted.
Command line interface: users type commands. Also needs regular updates.
Replies, but nothing is listening right now. Could become open later, so keep scanning.
Using storage, software or processing power over the internet instead of on your own equipment.
Microsoft 365, Google Drive, Amazon Web Services, OneDrive.
The organisation has less direct physical control over where its data and systems are stored.
Unauthorised access to computer material. Up to 2 years
Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further crime. Up to 5 years
Unauthorised acts to impair a computer or data, e.g. malware or DoS. Up to 10 years
3A (2006): making or supplying hacking tools, up to 2 years. 3ZA (2015): serious damage, e.g. to critical national infrastructure, 14 years to life
Pressuring an authorised person to let someone in, through bribery, social engineering or blackmail.
Real incidents rarely fit one category. Serious attacks cause overlapping losses.
The server a hacker uses to control the bots in a botnet.
Systems that distribute products and services, often linked to online shopping.
Payments to put things right for affected customers or partners, e.g. refunds and credit monitoring. Not fines.
Makes it a crime to access or change computer material without permission
Exploited the Windows Server service and built a large botnet. Lesson: patches, antivirus, network security.
Lawful basis: the person has freely and clearly agreed. Must be a clear, active choice, not a pre-ticked box
Lawful basis: the data is needed to deliver a contract, e.g. bank details to take a monthly payment
A payment owed when agreed goods or services can't be delivered.
The app, website or cloud dashboard used to control an IoT device. Weak authentication lets attackers take over.
Copper = electrical signals, can be tapped; fibre = light pulses, harder to tap but can be spliced.
Usernames and passwords. They must be protected and never shared.
A realistic risk that is likely to cause harm if it happens, not just a theoretical danger.
Essential services such as water, energy, communication and transport. Attacks can cripple whole cities.
A harmful script is saved on a page and runs in the browser of anyone who views it.
A severity score from 0 to 10. Higher = more serious, so fix it first.
Spying on systems to steal secrets for a military, political or economic advantage.
Attacking systems to damage or disrupt an enemy's operations.
Protecting computer systems, networks and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.
An action or event that tries to damage, steal or disrupt computer systems, networks or data.
Terrorist attacks that target computer systems to destroy them or disrupt the people who rely on them.
The damage or loss an organisation suffers when an attack successfully affects its systems, data or operations.
Organisations, governments and countries hacking each other for secret information and blocking each other's attacks.
Check doors, alarms and restricted areas are secure.
Staff can't access the information they need to work.
When sensitive or confidential data is lost, stolen or seen by someone who shouldn't have it.
Deleting or overwriting files so they're gone. Nothing is altered, just removed.
Data moving between the organisation, the internet and the provider. It could be intercepted, stolen or changed.
GDPR principle: only collect data you actually need (HOW MUCH you collect)
Deliberately altering or adding errors to AI training data, causing bias and errors in the AI.
Changing data instead of stealing it, for someone's benefit or to cause damage.
Deliberately altering data to cause damage, so a service or website works wrongly or shows wrong content.
Stealing confidential information, either by copying it (victim may not notice) or removing it completely.
Distributed denial of service: many infected computers flood a target at once from many locations.
Fake 'disconnect' frames knock a device off Wi-Fi; as it reconnects, the attacker captures login information.
A digitally manipulated or AI-made video that changes someone's face, voice or words to give a new meaning.
The username and password a device ships with. Attackers can guess or look them up.
Check credentials, verify identity, and call back on a number from your card or statement.
Spot attacks and unusual activity quickly.
Scan → Score → Prioritise → Track. Tracks each fix until it is done.
Domain Name System: turns domain names into IP addresses so browsers can load pages.
A request asking a DNS server for the IP address of a domain name.
A hacker inserts a fraudulent DNS entry, so requests for a real site go to a fake look-alike site.
Denial of service: one machine floods a target, often a web server, with traffic so it stops working or crashes.
Hackers take data and use it against the victim, e.g. threatening to sell or leak it as well as disrupting systems.
Publishing someone's private information online to cause them harm. Can be a form of sabotage.
Reasonable steps an organisation takes to prevent unauthorised access, e.g. MFA, patching and disabling leavers' accounts
49152–65535: used for temporary or private connections.
Listening to data sent through the air.
Attacking banks, financial systems or businesses to damage another country's economy.
Scrambling data so it can't be read without the key. USB drives and external hard drives should be encrypted.
Spoofed sites usually have no certificate, so the connection is unencrypted (cleartext) and the browser warns you.
An encryptor scrambles your files; a locker locks you out of the whole computer with a ransom screen.
When the manufacturer stops supporting an OS or device and stops providing security updates.
Still works normally, but no longer gets fixes for new vulnerabilities.
Every device connected to a network is another possible way in.
Data breach that exposed the personal information of millions of people after hackers got into company systems.
GDPR principle: treat people fairly and be open about what is collected and why
A Wi-Fi hotspot pretending to be a trusted network, so the attacker can see connected users' data.
Manipulated audio, video, images or documents used to cause mistrust, reputational damage or financial loss.
The tool misses a real vulnerability, giving a false sense of security. Usually worse than a false positive.
The tool flags a problem that isn't really there, so time is wasted.
No reply at all: a firewall is blocking it.
A gate between a trusted network and the internet that controls incoming and outgoing traffic using ports.
A list of blocked sources. Unrecognised IPs found in logs can be added to it.
Wrong firewall settings that leave unwanted access open to attackers.
Because a DoS comes from one location, a good firewall can detect it and cut the connection.
The built-in software in a device such as a router or access point. It needs updating.
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
Breaking a door, lock or the surrounding walls to get in.
Poor software design, operating system choices, poor user habits, poor checking and testing.
Changing how a website or public display looks, e.g. defacing it as a prank or for ransom.
The UK's intelligence, security and cyber agency, which supports the NCSC.
Data protection law that applies to any organisation handling personal data, whatever its size.
A tool that hides an artist's style from AI image generators.
Graphical user interface: point-and-click windows and icons. Needs regular updates like any OS.
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, network or data without the owner's permission.
Comparing the official hash with your file's hash. A match means the file hasn't been tampered with.
A file's 'digital fingerprint'. Change even one letter and it becomes completely different.
Shows the connection to the website is encrypted. Check for it before downloading.
An honest mistake that causes a security problem, e.g. sending confidential data to the wrong person.
Information Commissioner's Office: the UK regulator that fines organisations for breaking data protection law.
The Information Commissioner's Office: enforces UK GDPR, with fines up to £17.5m or 4% of turnover
Know what you need to protect: systems, data, people and risks.
Checking photo ID and its expiry date, and comparing the name and photo with the person.
Insecure Direct Object Reference: changing part of a URL (e.g. /profile/123 to /124) to see someone else's data.
Unofficial software that may miss security updates and could contain malware or a backdoor.
Pretending to be someone trustworthy, like a bank, IT support or a manager.
Pretending to be someone else, such as staff or an authorised visitor, to get access.
Impersonation = pretending to be someone. Coercion = pressuring someone who IS authorised.
A tested plan so people know what to do during a cyber attack, reducing delays and damage.
Default or wrong settings, e.g. storage that lets outsiders see sensitive files.
When a rival organisation bribes an employee to steal things like a client list or intellectual property.
Attacks on chemical plants, factories or food distribution systems.
The worm opens the device to other malware or turns off protection such as Windows Defender.
The worm copies itself until storage and memory fill up and the device crashes.
Used by TV remotes and older devices. Signals can be captured and replayed.
Targeting essential services like power, water, transport or communications to cause widespread disruption.
Attacker input, e.g. SQL commands typed into a form, gets run by the system.
A place users type into, such as login boxes, search bars and online forms.
What an organisation pays for insurance. They rise after a reported breach.
GDPR principle: keep data secure from unauthorised access, loss or damage
Ideas, designs and creations an organisation owns, which rivals may try to steal.
An organisation's valuable ideas, designs, inventions and information, such as trade secrets.
A risk from within an organisation caused by employees or insiders through error, poor practice, theft or deliberate sabotage.
Everyday devices connected to the internet, such as door locks, alarms and baby monitors.
Internet of Things: everyday devices that connect to a network to collect, send or receive data.
A unique number for every internet-connected device, used by other devices to find it.
When valuable ideas, designs or information are stolen or exposed without permission.
Spyware that records keystrokes to steal usernames, passwords and PINs.
No patches from the maker, or not installed, so a known vulnerability can be targeted for a long time.
The legal reason for using personal data. Organisations must pick one of six before they start, and tell people
GDPR principle: have a valid legal reason (lawful basis) to use the data
Ransomware that also threatens to publish your data: double extortion.
Users should only have the access they need to do their job, no more.
Users only have access to what they need, no more.
Costs from regulators, courts or others: fines, penalty payments, investigation costs and legal fees.
Lawful basis: the law requires it, e.g. keeping staff right-to-work documents
Lawful basis: a genuine business reason that doesn't override people's rights, e.g. CCTV in a car park
Publishing false statements that damage someone's reputation. Online, it can be a form of sabotage.
Disabling a leaver's accounts as soon as they leave, so they can't still get in.
A web address made to look real but isn't, e.g. gov.uk-repay.com or ee.uk.billing45.com.
People who smashed machines they saw as a threat. Data poisoning is called their digital version.
Got into big Silicon Valley tech offices dressed as a doughnut delivery driver: impersonation in action.
Attack that took down M&S services such as digital click & collect, shown in the BBC News report on the slides.
Faking a device's MAC address. It shows MAC addresses can't be trusted on their own.
Malicious code inside a macro that runs when an infected document is opened. Only enable macros from trusted sources.
Software designed to harm, disrupt, steal data from, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system or network.
A space with two doors where people are authenticated at both ends; only one person fits, so tailgating is impossible.
Production stops because the systems that control machines fail.
The part of a disk that starts the computer up. The target of a boot sector virus.
Device release → active updates → end-of-support → growing risks.
Software organisations use to manage and track their phones and tablets (standard term).
Links the organisation to its internet provider. Risk: poor set-up or missing updates.
Watching system and network activity to spot suspicious behaviour quickly and support investigations.
Review access logs, security passes and CCTV.
Logging in with more than one proof of identity, e.g. a password plus a code on your phone.
National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (part of NIST): creates standards-based solutions for organisations.
National Cyber Security Centre: UK, launched 2016, supported by GCHQ; gives advice, threat news and guidance.
Non-disclosure agreement: a legal contract that stops people sharing confidential information.
Carelessness, such as leaving a device unlocked or sharing a password, that can lead to a data breach.
Draws a map of every device on a network and spots rogue or unexpected devices.
A weakness in the technology and connections that make up a network.
Sharing passwords by email (especially with the file) lets anyone who gets the email open the data.
Near-field communication, used for contactless payments. Risks: skimming, relay attacks.
National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (part of NIST; your slide says 'Institute'), created 2008 to support education and industry partners.
A tool artists use to 'poison' their images so AI trained on them learns the wrong things.
National Institute of Standards and Technology: USA, created 1901; develops cyber security standards and the CSF.
NIST Cybersecurity Framework: used internationally to improve security practice.
Infects executable files when programs are not running.
Original equipment manufacturer: the company that makes the device and releases its system updates.
Accepts the connection: a service is listening.
System software that manages a device's hardware and lets applications run, e.g. Windows, Android, iOS.
When an attack disrupts normal running, so the organisation can't operate until systems and data are restored.
The direct hit to finances: cash flow problems, lost profits and higher insurance costs.
A weakness in people, policies or processes that makes attacks easier.
A weakness in an OS that could be exploited, especially when it is unsupported, unpatched or poorly secured.
Software not regularly updated, so it's vulnerable to new threats.
Open Web Application Security Project: non-profit, set up 2001, not linked to any government; improves software security.
A live document of the ten biggest security risks for developers of software and web applications.
A list of the most serious web application security risks.
A safe way to build database queries so user input is never run as code (standard prevention).
The worm steals data by installing backdoors and spyware, e.g. WannaCry.
An app storing passwords in an encrypted vault behind one master password.
A fix or update released to correct a known weakness.
A fix released by the manufacturer to correct a known weakness.
A policy that keeps software up to date.
An ethical hacker tries to break in, with permission, to prove the real-world impact of a weakness. Deep, targeted, mostly manual.
Read (view), write (add/save), execute (run) and modify/change (edit).
Any information that can identify a living person, on its own or combined with other data. PII = personally identifying information
Fake messages that trick people into clicking links or giving details. Poorly trained staff may not spot them.
Fake emails that look legitimate, with links to malware or sites that harvest usernames and passwords.
Fake messages that trick people into clicking links or giving away details such as passwords.
Staff are sent a fake phishing email; the IT team records who clicks or enters details.
A sense of urgency, not personalised, a link that seems 'off'.
Protecting computer systems, devices and data from unauthorised physical access, damage or theft.
Protecting devices, data, people and buildings from physical threats such as theft, damage or unauthorised access.
A physical control such as a door lock that restricts access to digital systems.
A trusted third party tries to get into restricted areas, e.g. following staff through a door.
The slides' exam method: name it, how it's exploited, what happens, how to reduce it.
Changes its code or signature while keeping its harmful function, so signature-based antivirus fails to spot it.
Devices connected without IT checks may not be monitored or firewalled: a route into the network.
A physical (e.g. USB) or logical connection point; logical ports are linked to network services.
A numbered "door" used by one type of traffic, e.g. port 80 = HTTP, port 443 = HTTPS.
21 = FTP (file transfer), 22 = SSH (secure remote access), 25 = SMTP (sending email), 53 = DNS.
FTP (file transfer). Risky because data is not encrypted.
SSH (secure remote admin).
80 = HTTP (web traffic); 443 = HTTPS (secure web traffic).
Remote Desktop. High risk if open to the internet: a password-guessing target.
Sends a request to each port and records the reply, to find out which ports are open, closed or filtered.
Scanning an IP address to find open ports and discover which services are running.
Phones and laptops are easily lost; worse if the device is used for multi-factor authentication.
Creating a deceptive scenario to get information, posing as a trusted person who can solve a fake problem.
A normal user gains higher-level (e.g. admin) access without permission.
Put safeguards in place, e.g. access control, training, updates.
Lawful basis: needed for an official or public task, e.g. the DVLA issuing driving licences
Devices like ATMs and supermarket payment machines, especially open to shoulder surfing.
Potentially unwanted program: bundled with free software; can steal details, slow the device and cause crashes.
GDPR principle: only use data for the purpose you told people (WHAT you do with it)
Two men got into BT's Prestel system with a found password; their conviction was overturned because hacking wasn't a crime. This led to the CMA
Locks or encrypts files and demands a ransom to restore access.
Restore systems and data to normal and learn from the incident.
1024–49151: used by specific applications or services.
Scans the registry for unauthorised or suspicious changes so they can be undone.
Portable storage such as USB drives. Easily lost or stolen, exposing sensitive data.
A rating from an independent system showing how an organisation is seen. It can be downgraded after an attack.
Damage to how an organisation is seen: loss of trust, negative reviews, lower reputation scores.
Stays in memory and infects applications as the user opens them.
Take action during an incident to contain it and limit damage.
An area, such as a server room, that only authorised people should enter.
A tool that turns an IP address back into a host name.
Removing access immediately when staff leave or change roles.
Used in door entry cards and tags. Risks: eavesdropping, cloning tags.

terms.term: Right not to be subject to automated decision-making
terms.def: The right to ask for a human to review a decision made by a computer
The right to see a copy of your data
The right to be told how and why your data is used
The right to get your data in a machine-readable format, e.g. to move to a new bank
The right to say "stop", e.g. to direct marketing
Gives attackers root-level privileges and can disable antivirus. Signs: slow apps, crashes, antivirus failing.
Sends data between networks. If taken over: redirects traffic, reads data, helps attackers move deeper.
Deliberately damaging equipment, data or systems to cause loss or disruption, e.g. a redundant worker damaging a server.
Deliberately damaging, disrupting or interfering with data, systems, devices or infrastructure to cause harm or stop them working.
Used by ships, planes and remote places. Long-distance signals can be intercepted.
Passwords saved in a browser can be used by hackers to get into banking, shopping and streaming accounts.
Fake pop-ups saying you have a virus, pushing you to download fake software. Can lead to identity theft.
Destroying or wiping storage devices properly so confidential data can't be recovered.
How seriously staff take security. A weak culture leads to ignored policies and unsafe practice.
A card or badge that unlocks restricted areas for authorised people.
A check that only authorised people have access to restricted areas and systems.
Checking the identity of visitors to reduce the risk of unauthorised access to a site.
Websites, apps or customer services go offline.
A common hashing method used to create hash values for downloads.
Reading security information by looking at someone's screen: up close, with binoculars, or via CCTV.
How traditional antivirus spots malware: by matching known code patterns. Fails against polymorphic viruses.
A Windows network service for sharing files. Its weakness was exploited by WannaCry.
SMS phishing: scam text messages, e.g. a fake parcel redelivery fee with a link.
Tricking people into giving away secure information. It relies on deception, not technical hacking.
The legal terms for using software. Breaking them, e.g. installing it on personal devices, can lead to fines.
A software control such as passwords, or blocking untrustworthy websites.
A weakness or flaw in software that could be exploited to cause harm, steal data or gain unauthorised access.
A targeted phishing attack on a carefully chosen person, with personalised language and wording.
Processor (hardware) weaknesses that could let attackers read data in memory.
A fake site that looks like the official one, used to steal passwords, bank and card details.
AI often struggles to draw human hands, which can give a fake image away.
Secretly monitors activity and captures data like passwords and keystrokes without consent.
Structured Query Language: how websites and apps communicate with databases.
Inserting malicious SQL code into input fields (login, search, forms) to trick the system into giving database access.
Database commands typed into a form or search box let an attacker read or change records.
Leaking personal data through SQL injection can break privacy laws like GDPR.
Spyware on a phone that tracks GPS location, calls, messages and internet use, and can record audio.
Enable automatic updates; keep anti-malware and firewall switched on; upgrade when unsupported.
GDPR principle: don't keep data longer than needed
Data needs protecting both when it's stored and when it's moving.
A request to an organisation to see a copy of the data it holds about you. It must usually respond within one month
One weak link can expose the whole chain: tampered safety data, counterfeit goods, delays, financial crises.
Connects devices in one part of a network. If compromised: attacker can watch traffic or change port settings.
Builds a detailed list of connected devices with their IP address, operating system and protocols.
An authorised person opens a door and an unauthorised person follows them in.
SQL injection attack; data on around 157,000 customers stolen; £400,000 ICO fine.
Provider administrators, engineers and support staff may have technical access to your systems and data.
Something or someone that could cause harm by exploiting a vulnerability, e.g. a hacker or malware.
The whole picture of cyber threats at a given time. It keeps changing.

terms.term: Threat vs vulnerability vs attack vector
terms.def: Threat = who/what wants to cause harm; vulnerability = the weakness; attack vector = the route in.
Third-party risk management: checking and managing the risks of relying on outside providers.
Confidential business information that gives a company an advantage, e.g. a recipe or product design.
Many bots send far more traffic at once, overloading a server rapidly.
The large amount of example data an AI system learns from.
Malware disguised as something harmless, e.g. hidden in unofficial games, apps or bootleg movies.
A reliable, official place to download software, e.g. the developer's own website.
A gate that lets one person through at a time, to stop tailgating.
A character (who they pretend to be) and a situation (the made-up problem).
The law that controls how organisations collect, store, use and share personal data, and gives people rights over their data
A device left alone, especially in public, that can be stolen or accessed.
Getting into a system or data you don't have permission to use.
Software not approved by the organisation. It may be unlicensed, incompatible or contain spyware or malware.
Accidentally deleting or changing data through human error. Not classed as sabotage.
Software without the latest fix installed, so a known weakness stays open.
An operating system that no longer receives security updates, so known vulnerabilities stay unfixed.
Google/Apple create the fix → the phone maker and network provider approve and release it.
Small and easily lost or stolen; anyone who has it may access the data on it.
Risks people create through mistakes, poor practices or weak processes.
Malware that spreads between computers by infecting files and software, damaging data and causing disruption.
Voice phishing: scam phone calls or voice messages, e.g. fake IT support asking for login details.
A system that logs visitors' names, entry times and reasons for visiting.
Visitors sign in, wear a temporary badge, are escorted at all times, and return the badge on exit.
Lawful basis: needed to protect someone's life, e.g. sharing allergy details with A&E
Virtual private network: a secure, encrypted connection over the internet.
A weakness in a system that can be exploited by cybercriminals to gain unauthorised access.
A weakness in a system that could be exploited, e.g. an unneeded open port or a missing patch.
Finding, listing and ranking (prioritising) the weaknesses in a system, network or app, before an attacker can use them.
Ransomware worm that infected over 200,000 computers worldwide and badly affected the NHS.
Ransomware exploiting Windows' SMB service; spread without opening a file; 200,000+ computers including the NHS.
Data sent without proper protection can be intercepted, read or changed.
E.g. a poor password-reset procedure or a hidden backdoor that attackers can exploit.
A site uses an old encryption protocol, so data sent to it could be intercepted.
Humans are usually the weakest link in security, which is why staff training is essential.
Both track users. Web beacons track behaviour on one page and can't be declined; tracking cookies can be declined.
Injects malicious code into web pages through browser weaknesses to steal usernames and passwords.
A digital certificate proving a site's identity. It should be valid before you download.
Automatically sends test requests to a website, tests for the OWASP Top 10 and produces a report.
0–1023: used by common network services.
Spear phishing aimed at high net-worth, powerful people such as a CEO.
Bypass logins; view, change or delete data; reach admin controls; steal customer data.

terms.term: Why DDoS is harder to stop
terms.def: It comes from many locations, which disguises its origin, so you can't just block one source.
They can contain sensitive or confidential data that criminals can access or extract.
Security is often weak, and every device is another access point into a home network.
Devices are small, cheap and low-powered, so they often have fewer security features.
They sit in the middle of the network, so one compromised device affects many others.
They release system updates; if they're slow or stop, devices stay vulnerable.
Cost, compatibility issues and older hardware.
It links the inside network to the outside world, and almost every outside attack crosses it.
Criminals adapt; geopolitics shifts; new laws and organisations appear; technology changes and creates new weaknesses.
Wireless networking. Attacked with fake access points and eavesdropping.
A database of settings for Windows, users, software and security, stored as keys and values. It does NOT store your files.
Lets devices join by Wi-Fi. A rogue or badly placed one can spread the network outside the building.
Gives internet access and Wi-Fi. Risks: default passwords, old firmware, weak encryption.
Self-replicating malware that spreads by itself between devices through email attachments, links or a LAN.
An attack using a previously unknown flaw. No patch exists yet, so it's especially risky.
A brand-new vulnerability not yet in the tool's database, with no fix, so automated tools miss it.
